catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic. ... 2.3 Stress. Stress is distinctive. Consider the following minimal pairs: ... Stress is a combination of pitch, force and length but pitch is the dominating element. Stress may occur on any syllable but the last syllable of words gets stress in a tiny minority of words only. No V.'V words have yet been found. Examples: ... 'V.CV head ... V.'CV mouth ... 'CV.CV.CV tongue ... CV.'CV.CV rain ... 'CV.CV bone ... CV.'CV palm wine ... V.CV.'CV star ... V.'CV.CV spear ... With some words stress has been found to vary, for example Imidol 'sand', Imidol 'sand'. ... [ch.1 (c) Adaptation in word stress and intonation contours:] Inanwatan has unpredictable, lexical word stress. Quite often the word stress of foreign words changes in borrowed words, e.g. regional Malay pandita>Inanwatan paditae '(male) minister'.

tone_statements.citation: Holton, Gary & Marian Klamer. 2018. The Papuan languages of East Nusantara and the Bird's Head. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 569-640. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton.
tone_statements.quote: Tone, in its various guises, is said to be one of the defining features of Papuan languages, but in the area under investigation here it is rare, and if it occurs, it has a low functional load. Some evidence for phonemic tone is found in the Bird’s Head isolate languages of Abun and Mpur. ... A more common feature of Papuan languages is a pitch-accent system which distinguishes one syllable of a word as more prominent than others. ... In some cases stress distinctions are phonemic. Lexical stress is even more distinctive in Inanwatan, where numerous minimal pairs can be identified, for example: meˈʔo ‘rope’ versus ˈmeʔo ‘wood’ and toˈʔo ‘palm wine’ versus ˈtoʔo ‘bone’ (de Vries 2004: 25).
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone attributed to Inanwatan; distinctive (lexical) word stress with minimal pairs, grouped by the authors with Papuan pitch accent/stress systems; tone in the region only in Abun and Mpur.

sources.note: Sec. 5.3.1 has a prosody passage stating that tone is rare in East Nusantara and the Bird's Head and, where present (Abun, Mpur), has low functional load; pitch accent/lexical-stress systems are more common, and Inanwatan is given as the clearest case of distinctive lexical stress with minimal pairs (from de Vries 2004: 25). It does not attribute tone to Inanwatan.

tone.quote: Inanwatan has a five vowel system (i, e, u, o, a) and 12 consonant phonemes: p, t, k, b, d, g, <I>, s, m, n, j, and the glottal stop. Inanwatan syllables can be subsumed under one type of syllable: (C)V{V). Stress is phonemic.
